title: Essence of Calculus, Chapter 1
hook: The opening promises that viewers will feel they could have invented calculus themselves, reframing a daunting subject as a natural discovery waiting to happen.

scenes.purpose: Establish the series and its radical promise: understanding over memorization

on_screen.desc: Video series strip with Chapter 1 highlighted in yellow
Welcome to Essence of Calculus
List of calculus rules flying into video thumbnails

scenes.transition: Series strip fades; pi-creatures remain as interlocutors
scenes.narration_gist: Rather than memorizing rules, the goal is for you to feel you could have invented calculus yourself.

scenes.purpose: Anchor the entire video in one concrete geometric question

on_screen.desc: Blue filled circle with radius line labeled R=3
Formula: Area = π R²
Question marks ???

scenes.transition: Pi-creature dismissed; circle stays center stage
scenes.narration_gist: We start with just you and a circle of radius 3, asking where the area formula actually comes from.

scenes.purpose: Introduce the key conceptual move: slicing into concentric rings

on_screen.desc: Circle decomposed into rainbow concentric rings
One isolated ring shifted right with radius label r
Area ? label next to isolated ring

scenes.transition: All rings remain; one ring duplicated and moved to right half
scenes.narration_gist: Slicing the circle into concentric rings respects its symmetry, and math rewards symmetry.

scenes.purpose: Approximate each ring as a rectangle and introduce dr notation

on_screen.desc: Ring unwrapped into a near-rectangle
Width brace labeled 2πr, height brace labeled dr
Area ≈ 2πr · dr

scenes.transition: Isolated ring animates into straightened rectangle; original circle kept faint at left
scenes.narration_gist: Unwrapping the ring gives a rectangle of width 2πr and thickness dr, so its area is approximately 2πr·dr.

scenes.purpose: Translate the sum of ring areas into a visual of rectangles under a graph

on_screen.desc: Coordinate axes with r on x-axis; stacked colored rectangles of width dr
Line graph of 2πr touching rectangle tops
Area ≈ 2πr · dr for each ring

scenes.transition: Rings from circle transform (path-arc animation) into upright rectangles on the graph
scenes.narration_gist: Each ring's area becomes a thin rectangle on a graph, and together they approximate the area under the line 2πr.

scenes.purpose: Let dr shrink to zero, revealing the triangle whose area is exactly πR²

on_screen.desc: Increasingly thin Riemann rectangles converging under 2πr line
Triangle with base 3 and height 2π·3 shaded under the line
½ · base · height = π · 3²

scenes.transition: Rectangles visually merge into the triangle; formula written in corner
scenes.narration_gist: As dr approaches zero the rectangles' total area becomes exactly the triangle under the graph, giving πR².

scenes.purpose: Name the two big ideas just demonstrated: integrals and the area-under-curve reframe

on_screen.desc: Hard problem → Sum of small values → Area under a graph
Graph of 2πr with filled triangle
General principle: any such sum = area under some graph

scenes.transition: Triangle kept; new text overlay summarizes the principle abstractly
scenes.narration_gist: This strategy—approximate with thin rectangles then let them shrink—turns hard sum problems into area-under-graph problems, i.e., integrals.

scenes.purpose: Introduce a harder case (parabola) to motivate derivatives as the inverse tool

on_screen.desc: Parabola x² with shaded area from 0 to variable x
Mystery function A(x) label with brace
Thin sliver dA highlighted between x and x+dx

scenes.transition: Triangle/circle cleared; new axes and parabola drawn fresh
scenes.narration_gist: Now imagine the area under x² as a mystery function A(x); nudging x by dx produces a sliver dA ≈ x²·dx.

scenes.purpose: Define derivative as the ratio dA/dx and show it equals the graph height

on_screen.desc: Equation dA/dx ≈ x²
Parabola with sliver shrinking as dx→0
Derivative: ratio of tiny output change to tiny input change

scenes.transition: Sliver animation loops with decreasing dx; equation stays fixed on right
scenes.narration_gist: The ratio dA/dx approaches x² as dx shrinks—this ratio is called the derivative of A.

scenes.purpose: Name the Fundamental Theorem and close with the series promise

on_screen.desc: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus label
Integrals ↔ Derivatives (inverse relationship)
Series roadmap: details on derivatives, integrals, and more ahead

scenes.transition: All prior visuals fade; clean text statement of the theorem
scenes.narration_gist: The derivative of the area function gives back the original graph—integrals and derivatives are inverses, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

lessons: Anchor an abstract topic in one concrete, familiar object before introducing any formalism.
Use physical transformation animations (unwrapping, sliding, morphing) to make algebraic approximations feel inevitable rather than imposed.
Keep a persistent visual artifact (the circle or the graph) on screen while layering new concepts on top of it, so viewers always know where they are.
Introduce notation only after the idea it names has already been seen visually, so the symbol feels like a label rather than a definition.
Stage the payoff as a visual surprise (rectangles collapsing into a triangle) so the result feels discovered, not just derived.
Close each major insight by naming the general principle it illustrates, then immediately gesture toward the next open question to sustain momentum.
tags: calculus integral derivative area circle pi limit slice
